title: Professional and scientific industry the only one where pay continues to match rising prices
meta_description: Article exploring how wage growth in different industries compares with rising prices

breadcrumb.text: Professional and scientific industry the only one where pay continues to match rising prices

lede: Public administration and education have seen some of the lowest pay growth during 2022

body.text: 23 November 2022

Prices in the UK have been rising steeply since the end of 2021. In October 2022, [the inflation rate including owner occupier’s housing costs (CPIH), reached 9.6%](https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/inflationandpriceindices/bulletins/consumerpriceinflation/october2022). This means that the prices of goods and services across the country were on average 9.6% higher than in October the year before. This is the highest CPIH rate since December 1980, according to historical estimates.

Average wages in the UK have risen at a slower pace than prices. In July to September 2022, regular wages rose by 5.7% year-on-year, and total pay, which includes bonuses, rose 6.0%. This means that pay has fallen in real terms: workers need a larger proportion of their wages to buy the same goods.

Many are feeling financial effects as a result. In late October and early November 2022, 93% of adults in Great Britain [said the cost of living was an important issue facing the UK](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/wellbeing/bulletins/publicopinionsandsocialtrendsgreatbritain/26octoberto6november2022), and 91% said their cost of living had gone up compared with a year ago.

Not all workers have seen prices rise faster than their pay during the year. In some industries, such as professional and scientific or property, pay growth was above inflation before and during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, and continued to exceed inflation in early 2022.

However, as inflation continued increasing steeply during 2022, regular wage growth fell behind inflation in all industries except professional and scientific (which includes businesses covering areas such as legal services, management, engineering and scientific research).
In other industries, such as public administration and education, pay growth has been below inflation since the second half of 2021.

Workers within each industry have also been affected differently depending on their wages. Those [on lower pay](https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/earningsandworkinghours/bulletins/lowandhighpayuk/2022) will feel the impact of wage growth falling behind inflation and the resulting increased cost of living more acutely.

body.box_text: You can use [our calculator](https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/inflationandpriceindices/articles/areyourwageskeepingupwithinflation/2017-06-20) to see how inflation has affected the value of your pay compared with last year, and what increase would be necessary for your wages to keep pace with inflation.

body.h2: Wage growth in the professional and scientific industry has remained above inflation throughout 2022
body.text: Wage growth in the professional and scientific industry has remained above inflation throughout 2022

body.h2: Wage growth in the professional and scientific industry has remained above inflation throughout 2022
body.text: Regular wage growth in the professional and scientific industry has sat above inflation since November 2018. It remained so during the coronavirus pandemic and has kept pace with prices as they have risen over the last year.

body.h2: Wage growth in the professional and scientific industry has remained above inflation throughout 2022
body.text: Since May to July 2022, the professional and scientific industry has been the only one where regular wage growth (excluding bonuses) has remained higher than inflation; sitting at 10.1% in July to September 2022. This means average wages in the industry in this period were 10.1% higher than the same period the previous year.

body.h2: Wage growth in the professional and scientific industry has remained above inflation throughout 2022
body.text: Wage growth in other industries, such as property, information and communication, retail, and finance, also sat largely above inflation in recent years. However, between January to March 2022 and April to June 2022, rising inflation outpaced regular wage growth in all of these industries.

body.h2: Bonus pay boosts wages in some industries, especially in finance
body.text: Bonus pay boosts wages in some industries, especially in finance

body.h2: Bonus pay boosts wages in some industries, especially in finance
body.text: Although regular pay growth in finance fell below inflation in January to March 2022, higher bonuses have compensated. Total pay (which includes bonus pay) grew faster than prices until the three months to June 2022. In the three months to September 2022, it sat below inflation, at 6.3%.

body.h2: Bonus pay boosts wages in some industries, especially in finance
body.text: The finance industry has the highest average regular pay (£1,147 per week in the three months to September 2022). It also offers high bonuses, which represent a large proportion of total pay, especially during "bonus season". This is typically between December and March.

body.h2: Bonus pay boosts wages in some industries, especially in finance
body.text: As inflation started rising steeply at the end of 2021, total pay growth in finance also rose steeply to 15.9% in October to December 2021. This is the highest rate since the cap on bankers’ bonuses was introduced in the UK in 2013.

body.h2: Record vacancy numbers may be another reason behind wage growth
body.text: Record vacancy numbers may be another reason behind wage growth

body.h2: Record vacancy numbers may be another reason behind wage growth
body.text: UK job vacancies reached a record high of 1.3 million in March to May 2022. In August to October 2022, there were 54% more vacancies than pre-coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic (January to March 2020).

body.h2: Record vacancy numbers may be another reason behind wage growth
body.text: Worker shortages (manifested in high numbers of vacancies) can lead to wage increases, as employers compete to attract or keep workers. This could partly explain high wage growth in some industries in early 2022.

body.h2: Record vacancy numbers may be another reason behind wage growth
body.text: Four of the five industries where wage growth stayed above inflation in early 2022 (professional and scientific, information and communication, retail and finance), also had vacancy rates in June 2022 that were 1.5 or more percentage points higher than a year before. The vacancy rate is the percentage of jobs which remain vacant. This can be seen in the following chart.

body.text: Hospitality also saw a big increase in both the vacancy rate and wages in the year to June 2022. The hospitality workforce was highly disrupted by the coronavirus pandemic and had a relatively high number of jobs furloughed. Therefore, interpreting recent wage growth data in this industry is particularly complicated, as we will explore further.

Around a fifth of hospitality businesses reported increasing wages in Summer 2022, 23% in May and June and 20% in June and July. This is according to the Office for National Statistics’ (ONS’) Business Insights and Conditions Survey (BICS) as published in our [Business insights and impact on the UK economy: 11 August 2022 bulletin](https://www.ons.gov.uk/businessindustryandtrade/business/businessservices/bulletins/businessinsightsandimpactontheukeconomy/11august2022) and [Business insights and impact on the UK economy: 25 August 2022 bulletin.](https://www.ons.gov.uk/businessindustryandtrade/business/businessservices/bulletins/businessinsightsandimpactontheukeconomy/25august2022)

body.h2: Public sector industries among those with lowest wage growth
body.text: Public sector industries among those with lowest wage growth

body.h2: Public sector industries among those with lowest wage growth
body.text: Regular pay growth in the public sector was 2.2% in July to September 2022, while in the private sector it was 6.6%. This is both the largest private sector pay growth and the largest gap between public and private pay growth on record (since January 2000), excluding the height of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

body.h2: Public sector industries among those with lowest wage growth
body.text: Industries with more public sector jobs, such as education and public administration, have seen some of the lowest pay growth in 2022, along with arts and recreation, mining, and power and water.

body.h2: Public sector industries among those with lowest wage growth
body.text: The health industry has seen higher pay growth than education and public administration throughout 2022, although it has remained below inflation. In July to September 2022, regular wage growth in the health industry was 4.7%, compared with 2.9% in education and 3.6% in public administration.

body.h2: Public sector industries among those with lowest wage growth
body.text: Industries that have seen the largest pay growth in recent months – professional and scientific, property, information and communication, retail and finance – are mainly in the private sector.

body.h2: Public sector industries among those with lowest wage growth
body.text: Workers in the arts and entertainment industry have experienced the largest falls in wages in 2022. Although part of this fall can be explained by [base effects](https://blog.ons.gov.uk/2021/07/15/far-from-average-how-covid-19-has-impacted-the-average-weekly-earnings-data/), this is particularly problematic as [a fifth (21%) of workers in the arts and entertainment industry are on low pay](https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/earningsandworkinghours/bulletins/lowandhighpayuk/2022#those-most-affected-by-low-pay) (earning less than two-thirds of the national median hourly earnings). Public administration and education have far fewer workers on low pay, at 1% and 5%, respectively.

body.h2: Retail, hospitality and arts and recreation industries among worst affected by coronavirus lockdowns
body.text: Retail, hospitality and arts and recreation industries among worst affected by coronavirus lockdowns

body.h2: Retail, hospitality and arts and recreation industries among worst affected by coronavirus lockdowns
body.text: Industries that experienced the most disruption to the workforce during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, such as retail, hospitality, and arts and entertainment, have seen large swings in average pay and pay growth over recent years. This makes understanding trends in wage growth more complicated.

body.h2: Retail, hospitality and arts and recreation industries among worst affected by coronavirus lockdowns
body.text: One factor that affected average wages during the coronavirus pandemic was workforce composition. A relatively large amount of low paid workers lost their jobs, which pushes up average wages even if no workers received pay rises. [This is known as a compositional effect.](https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/earningsandworkinghours/articles/howfurloughandchangesintheemployeeworkforcehaveaffectedearningsgrowthduringthecoronaviruscovid19pandemicuk2020to2021/2022-04-29)

body.h2: Retail, hospitality and arts and recreation industries among worst affected by coronavirus lockdowns
body.text: Another factor was furlough. [The Coronavirus Job Retention Scheme (CJRS)](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/claim-for-wages-through-the-coronavirus-job-retention-scheme) supported businesses in paying their employees during the coronavirus pandemic. This decreased earnings for many workers, [who were paid 80% of their salaries up to £2,500 per month](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/changes-to-the-coronavirus-job-retention-scheme/changes-to-the-coronavirus-job-retention-scheme) (employers could choose to top it up to 100%). Over 11.7 million jobs were covered by the scheme between 19 March 2020 and 30 September 2021, and [almost 4 in 10 (38%) were in the retail or hospitality industries](https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/coronavirus-job-retention-scheme-statistics-16-december-2021/coronavirus-job-retention-scheme-statistics-16-december-2021#furlough-by-industry).

body.h2: Retail, hospitality and arts and recreation industries among worst affected by coronavirus lockdowns
body.text: These compositional and furlough effects are continuing to complicate wage growth data even after restrictions have lifted, as growth is measured by year-on-year change. This is known as [a base effect](https://blog.ons.gov.uk/2021/07/15/far-from-average-how-covid-19-has-impacted-the-average-weekly-earnings-data/).

body.h2: Retail, hospitality and arts and recreation industries among worst affected by coronavirus lockdowns
body.text: In the hospitality industry, for example, regular pay growth hit 12.9% in the three months to June 2021. This high growth is largely a result of average wages in hospitality being unusually low the same period the year before, when lockdowns were in place (negative 11.9% pay growth in June 2020).

body.h2: Retail, hospitality and arts and recreation industries among worst affected by coronavirus lockdowns
body.text: In addition, around 159,000 hospitality employees were still furloughed in September 2021, which partly explains the higher wage growth (6.3%) in the three months to September 2022, although this was below inflation.

body.h2: Retail, hospitality and arts and recreation industries among worst affected by coronavirus lockdowns
body.text: Average weekly earnings in hospitality are the lowest of any industry, at £277.66. [Within the hospitality industry, 44% of workers are in low pay](https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/earningsandworkinghours/bulletins/lowandhighpayuk/2022). The impact of falling wages is particularly acute for them. Despite the industry seeing slightly higher wage growth than some others, it is unlikely that hospitality workers are better protected against rising prices.

body.h2: Retail, hospitality and arts and recreation industries among worst affected by coronavirus lockdowns
body.text: Other industries, such as retail and construction, have experienced similar volatility in pay growth since the coronavirus pandemic. These industries were also closed for significant periods during pandemic lockdowns and had high levels of participation in the furlough scheme.

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: Measuring the data

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: Wage growth

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: Wage data in this article come from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) Monthly Wages and Salaries Survey, which is published in the [Average weekly earnings in Great Britain: November 2022 bulletin](https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/employmentandemployeetypes/bulletins/averageweeklyearningsingreatbritain/november2022).

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: Wages are expressed in nominal terms (not adjusted for inflation). Annual wage growth is calculated using three-monthly averages of monthly average weekly earnings (AWE). Three-monthly averages improve the reliability of the data, which is volatile at industry level, and are also taken in the headline figures in the ONS Average weekly earnings in Great Britain bulletin.

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: Inflation

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: Inflation data in this article come from the [ONS Consumer price inflation, UK: October 2022 bulletin](https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/inflationandpriceindices/bulletins/consumerpriceinflation/october2022).

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: Inflation is measured using the Consumer Prices Index including owner-occupiers' housing costs (CPIH), rather than the Consumer Prices Index (CPI), because it is the most comprehensive measure of inflation and incorporates costs associated with owning, maintaining and living in one's own home, which are significant costs for many households.

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: Inflation rate figures are calculated using a three-monthly average index CPIH. This is done for comparability with the average weekly earnings figures we present. CPIH figures in this article are therefore slightly different to the ones published in the ONS Consumer Price Inflation bulletin, which are calculated using monthly data.

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: Vacancy rates

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: Vacancy data in this article come from the ONS Vacancy Survey. Employee jobs data come from the ONS Workforce Jobs (WFJ) dataset, which estimates employee job numbers from employer surveys. The latest release of workforce jobs includes data up to June 2022. The vacancies and employee jobs data in this article are published in the [ONS Vacancies and jobs in the UK bulletin.](https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/employmentandemployeetypes/bulletins/jobsandvacanciesintheuk/october2022)

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: The vacancy rate in this article is defined as the number of vacancies as a percentage of employee jobs plus vacancies. This definition is different from the vacancy rates published in the monthly Vacancies and jobs in the UK bulletin.

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: All data used in the article are three-month averages, apart from workforce jobs employee numbers, which are collected every three months.

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: Industry classification

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: The industry breakdown used for this analysis is based on the [UK Standard Industrial Classification (SIC)](https://onsdigital.github.io/dp-classification-tools/standard-industrial-classification/ONS_SIC_hierarchy_view.html).
